From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-IAU-USGS-1)

* Mercurian: 414 craters (7.9%)
* Lunar: 1,624 craters (31.1%)
* Martian: 1,092 craters (20.9%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.2%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (22.9%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg/250px-Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_1.jpg)

The [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom")

This is a partial **list of recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom**, listed chronologically within the aspect of life in which each recipient is or was renowned.

The [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") is awarded by the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") to "any person recommended to the President for award of the Medal or any person selected by the President upon his own initiative".[[1]](#cite_note-1) Before 1970, honorees were either selected by the president or recommended to them by the [Distinguished Civilian Service Awards Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Civilian_Service_Awards_Board "Distinguished Civilian Service Awards Board").[[2]](#cite_note-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_recipients&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Typically the medal is bestowed upon the recipient by the sitting president who has chosen them. However, the first recipients selected by president [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") before [his assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy "Assassination of John F. Kennedy") were formally awarded by his successor in office, [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson").[[3]](#cite_note-id26165-3)

President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") awarded 118 medals, the most of any president, followed by President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") with 89 medal recipients.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Three people—[Ellsworth Bunker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellsworth_Bunker "Ellsworth Bunker"), [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell"), and [Ben Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Carson "Ben Carson")—are two-time recipients of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Powell received his second award with distinction, while Bunker was given both of his awards with distinction.[[5]](#cite_note-2ndPMoF-5)

Eight presidents have themselves received the medal posthumously, post-presidency, or prior to being elected:

* [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") (1963, posthumously)
* [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson") (1980, posthumously)
* [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") (1993, with distinction)
* [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford") (1999)
* [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") (1999)
* [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") (2011)
* [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") (2013)
* [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") (2017, as Vice President; with distinction)

In 2015, Obama stated that there was no precedent to revoke a Presidential Medal of Freedom, regarding the award given to stand-up comedian and actor [Bill Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby "Bill Cosby").[[6]](#cite_note-6) After being awarded the medal in 2002 by Obama's predecessor, [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), Cosby was [convicted of multiple counts of sexual assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby_sexual_assault_cases "Bill Cosby sexual assault cases"), though the convictions were later overturned.[[7]](#cite_note-ctv-overturned-7)

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is related to, but distinct from, the [Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medal_of_Freedom_(1945) "Medal of Freedom (1945)"), an earlier award issued between 1945 and 1963 to honor US civilian contributions to [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

In 2022 at the age of 25, athlete and activist [Simone Biles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simone_Biles "Simone Biles") became the youngest person to receive the award.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

### Declinations of the award

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=List_of_Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom_recipients&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Declinations of the award")]

[Bill Belichick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Belichick "Bill Belichick"), coach of the [New England Patriots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Patriots "New England Patriots"), was offered the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), and initially accepted it, but changed his mind and turned down the medal after the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack").[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Country musician [Dolly Parton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_Parton "Dolly Parton") turned down the medal twice from Donald Trump. Parton said she turned it down the first time because her husband was ill, and the second time because of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[10]](#cite_note-10)

**Aaron Copland** ([/ˈkoʊplənd/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*KOHP-lənd*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) November 14, 1900 – December 2, 1990) was an American composer, critic, writer, teacher, pianist, and conductor of his own and other American music. Copland was referred to by his peers and critics as the "Dean of American Music". The open, slowly changing harmonies in much of his music are typical of what many consider the sound of American music, evoking the vast American landscape and pioneer spirit. He is best known for the works he wrote in the 1930s and 1940s in a deliberately accessible style often referred to as "populist" and which he called his "vernacular" style.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack1999186-3) Works in this vein include the ballets *[Appalachian Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Spring "Appalachian Spring")*, *[Billy the Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_the_Kid_(ballet) "Billy the Kid (ballet)")* and *[Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodeo_(ballet) "Rodeo (ballet)")*, his *[Fanfare for the Common Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanfare_for_the_Common_Man "Fanfare for the Common Man")* and [Third Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._3_(Copland) "Symphony No. 3 (Copland)"). In addition to his ballets and orchestral works, he produced music in many other genres, including chamber music, vocal works, opera, and film scores.

After some initial studies with composer [Rubin Goldmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_Goldmark "Rubin Goldmark"), Copland traveled to Paris, where he first studied with [Isidor Philipp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidor_Philipp "Isidor Philipp") and [Paul Vidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Vidal "Paul Vidal"), then with noted pedagogue [Nadia Boulanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadia_Boulanger "Nadia Boulanger"). He studied three years with Boulanger, whose eclectic approach to music inspired his own broad taste. Determined upon his return to the U.S. to make his way as a full-time composer, Copland gave lecture-recitals, wrote works on commission and did some teaching and writing. But he found that composing orchestral music in a [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism_(music) "Modernism (music)") style, which he had adopted while studying abroad, was unprofitable, particularly in light of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"). He shifted in the mid-1930s to a more accessible musical style that mirrored the German idea of *[Gebrauchsmusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gebrauchsmusik "Gebrauchsmusik")* ("music for use"), music that could serve utilitarian and artistic purposes. During the Depression years, he traveled extensively to Europe, Africa, and Mexico, formed an important friendship with Mexican composer [Carlos Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Chávez "Carlos Chávez"), and began composing his signature works.

During the late 1940s, Copland became aware that [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky") and other fellow composers had begun to study [Arnold Schoenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schoenberg "Arnold Schoenberg")'s use of [twelve-tone (serial) techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-tone_technique "Twelve-tone technique"). After he had been exposed to the works of French composer [Pierre Boulez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulez "Pierre Boulez"), he incorporated serial techniques into his *Piano Quartet* (1950), *Piano Fantasy* (1957), *[Connotations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connotations_(Copland) "Connotations (Copland)")* for orchestra (1961), and *[Inscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inscape_(Copland) "Inscape (Copland)")* for orchestra (1967). Unlike Schoenberg, Copland used his tone rows in much the same fashion as his tonal material—as sources for melodies and harmonies, rather than as complete statements in their own right, except for crucial events from a structural point of view. From the 1960s onward, Copland's activities turned more from composing to conducting. He became a frequent guest conductor of orchestras in the U.S. and the UK and made a series of recordings of his music, primarily for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records").

## Life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Copland&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

### Early years

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Copland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Aaron Copland was born in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), New York, on November 14, 1900.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199915-4) He was the youngest of five children in a [Conservative Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Jewish "Conservative Jewish") immigrant family of [Lithuanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Jews "Lithuanian Jews") origin.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198419-5) While emigrating from Russia to the United States, Copland's father, Harris Morris Copland, lived and worked in Scotland for two to three years to pay for his boat fare to the United States. It was there that Copland's father may have [Anglicized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicized "Anglicized") his surname "Kaplan" to "Copland", though Copland himself believed for many years that the change had been caused by an [Ellis Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Island "Ellis Island") immigration official when his father entered the country.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199915-4)[[6]](#cite_note-Cone-6) Copland was unaware until late in his life that the family name had been Kaplan, his parents having never told him.[[6]](#cite_note-Cone-6) Throughout his childhood, Copland and his family lived above his parents' Brooklyn shop, H. M. Copland's, at 628 Washington Avenue (which Aaron later called "a kind of neighborhood [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's")"),[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199916-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) on the corner of Dean Street and Washington Avenue,[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoss2007266-9) and most of the children helped out in the store. His father was a staunch Democrat. The family members were active in [Congregation Baith Israel Anshei Emes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_Baith_Israel_Anshei_Emes "Congregation Baith Israel Anshei Emes"), where Aaron celebrated his [bar mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_mitzvah "Bar mitzvah"),[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199926-10) for which he studied under [Israel Goldfarb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Goldfarb "Israel Goldfarb").[[11]](#cite_note-jmrc-11) Not especially athletic, the sensitive young man became an avid reader and often read [Horatio Alger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Alger "Horatio Alger") stories on his front steps.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195315-12)

Copland's father had no musical interest. His mother, Sarah Mittenthal Copland, sang, played the piano, and arranged music lessons for her children.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199919-13) Copland had four older siblings: two brothers, Ralph and Leon, and two sisters, Laurine and Josephine.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Of his siblings, his oldest brother Ralph was the most advanced musically; he was proficient on the violin. Laurine had the strongest connection with Aaron; she gave him his first piano lessons, promoted his musical education, and supported him in his musical career.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199919-13) A student at the Metropolitan Opera School and frequent opera-goer, Laurine also brought home [libretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libretti "Libretti") for Aaron to study.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195317-16) Copland attended [Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boys_High_School_(Brooklyn) "Boys High School (Brooklyn)") and in the summer went to various camps. Most of his early exposure to music was at Jewish weddings and ceremonies, and occasional family musicales.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199926-10)

Copland began writing songs at the age of eight and a half.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17) His earliest notated music, about seven bars he wrote when age 11, was for an opera scenario he created and called *Zenatello*.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17)[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199932-18) From 1913 to 1917 he took piano lessons with Leopold Wolfsohn, who taught him the standard classical fare.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17) Copland's first public music performance was at a [Wanamaker's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanamaker's "Wanamaker's") recital.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195318-19)[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198423-20) By age 15, after attending a concert by Polish composer-pianist [Ignacy Jan Paderewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignacy_Jan_Paderewski "Ignacy Jan Paderewski"), Copland decided to become a composer.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199933-21) At 16, he heard his first symphony, at the [Brooklyn Academy of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Academy_of_Music "Brooklyn Academy of Music").[[22]](#cite_note-nyclgbtsites.org-22) After attempts to further his music study from a [correspondence course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correspondence_course "Correspondence course"), C

**Edward Kennedy** "**Duke**" **Ellington** (April 29, 1899 – May 24, 1974) was an American [jazz pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_piano "Jazz piano"), composer, and leader of his eponymous [jazz orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") from 1924 through the rest of his life. Music critic [Ralph J. Gleason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_J._Gleason "Ralph J. Gleason") called him "America's most important composer".[[2]](#cite_note-NYTObit-2)

Born and raised in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), Ellington was based in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") from the mid-1920s and gained a national profile through his orchestra's appearances at the [Cotton Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_Club "Cotton Club") in [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"). A master at writing miniatures for the three-minute [78 rpm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph_record#78_rpm_disc_developments "Phonograph record") recording format, Ellington wrote or collaborated on more than one thousand compositions; his extensive body of work is the largest recorded personal jazz legacy, and many of his pieces have become [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"). He also recorded songs written by his bandsmen, such as [Juan Tizol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Tizol "Juan Tizol")'s "[Caravan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravan_(Juan_Tizol_and_Duke_Ellington_song) "Caravan (Juan Tizol and Duke Ellington song)")", which brought a [Spanish tinge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_tinge "Spanish tinge") to [big band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_band "Big band") jazz.

At the end of the 1930s, Ellington began a nearly thirty-year collaboration with composer-arranger-pianist [Billy Strayhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Strayhorn "Billy Strayhorn"), whom he called his writing and arranging companion.[[3]](#cite_note-3) With Strayhorn, he composed multiple extended compositions, or suites, as well as many short pieces. For a few years at the beginning of Strayhorn's involvement, Ellington's orchestra featured bassist [Jimmy Blanton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Blanton "Jimmy Blanton") and tenor saxophonist [Ben Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Webster "Ben Webster"), and reached what many claim to be a creative peak for the group.[[4]](#cite_note-4) Some years later, following a low-profile period, an appearance by Ellington and his orchestra at the [Newport Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Jazz_Festival "Newport Jazz Festival") in July 1956 led to a major revival and regular world tours. Ellington recorded for most American record companies of his era, performed in and scored several films, and composed a handful of stage musicals.

Although a pivotal figure in the [history of jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), in the opinion of [Gunther Schuller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunther_Schuller "Gunther Schuller") and [Barry Kernfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Kernfeld "Barry Kernfeld"), "the most significant composer of the genre",[[5]](#cite_note-GroveJazz-5) Ellington himself embraced the phrase "beyond category", considering it a liberating principle, and referring to his music as part of the more general category of American music.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Ellington was known for his inventive use of the orchestra, or big band, as well as for his eloquence and charisma. He was awarded a posthumous [Pulitzer Prize Special Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_Special_Citations_and_Awards "Pulitzer Prize Special Citations and Awards") for music [in 1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Pulitzer_Prize#Other_awards "1999 Pulitzer Prize").[[7]](#cite_note-pulitzer-7)

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Duke_Ellington&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Ellington was born on April 29, 1899, to James Edward Ellington and Daisy (*née*  Kennedy) Ellington in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Both of his parents were pianists. Daisy primarily played [parlor songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlour_music "Parlour music") and James preferred operatic [arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria").[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrothers201810-8) They lived with Daisy's parents at 2129 Ida Place (now Ward Place) NW, in D.C.'s [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_(Washington,_D.C.) "West End (Washington, D.C.)") neighborhood.[[9]](#cite_note-Lawrence-1-9) Duke's father was born in [Lincolnton, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincolnton,_North_Carolina "Lincolnton, North Carolina"), on April 15, 1879, and in 1886, moved to D.C. with his parents.[[10]](#cite_note-Lawrence-2-10) Daisy Kennedy was born in Washington, D.C., on January 4, 1879, the daughter of two former [American slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States").[[9]](#cite_note-Lawrence-1-9)[[11]](#cite_note-11) James Ellington made blueprints for the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy").

When Ellington was a child, his family showed racial pride and support in their home, as did many other families. African Americans in D.C. worked to protect their children from the era's [Jim Crow laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Crow_laws "Jim Crow laws").[[12]](#cite_note-12)

At the age of seven, Ellington began taking piano lessons from Marietta Clinkscales.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrothers201810-8) Daisy surrounded her son with dignified women to reinforce his manners and teach him elegance. His childhood friends noticed that his casual, offhand manner and dapper dress gave him the bearing of a young nobleman,[[13]](#cite_note-Terkel-13) so they began calling him "Duke". Ellington credited his friend Edgar McEntee for the nickname: "I think he felt that in order for me to be eligible for his constant companionship, I should have a title. So he called me Duke."[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Though Ellington took piano lessons, he was more interested in [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball"). "President [[Theodore] Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt") would come on his horse sometimes, and "stop and watch us play", he recalled.[[15]](#cite_note-15) Ellington went to [Armstrong Technical High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendship_Armstrong_Academy "Friendship Armstrong Academy") in Washington, D.C. His first job was selling peanuts at [Washington Senators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Senators_(1901–1960) "Washington Senators (1901–1960)") baseball games.

**John Ernst Steinbeck** ([/ˈstaɪnbɛk/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*STYNE-bek*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); February 27, 1902 – December 20, 1968) was an American writer and novelist. He won the [1962 Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "1962 Nobel Prize in Literature") "for his realistic and imaginative writings, combining as they do sympathetic humor and keen social perception".[[2]](#cite_note-Literature1962-2) He has been called "a giant of American letters".[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Why_do_children_study_Of_Mice_and_Men?-4) One of the most widely read authors of the 20th century, he was also an independent journalist and war correspondent during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") and the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War").

During his writing career, he authored 33 books, with one book coauthored alongside [Edward Ricketts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Ricketts "Edward Ricketts"), including 16 novels, 6 [non-fiction books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction_book "Non-fiction book"), and 2 [collections of short stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collections_of_short_stories "Collections of short stories"). **Martha Graham** (May 11, 1894 – April 1, 1991)[[1]](#cite_note-1) was an American modern dancer, teacher and choreographer responsible for creating the [Graham technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_technique "Graham technique").[[2]](#cite_note-TIME-2)

Graham danced and taught for over seventy years. She was the first dancer to perform at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), travel abroad as a cultural ambassador, and receive the highest civilian award of the US: the [Presidential Medal of Freedom with Distinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom"). In her lifetime she received honors including the [Key to the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") of Paris and Japan's Imperial [Order of the Precious Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Precious_Crown "Order of the Precious Crown").

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Martha_Graham&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Graham was born in [Allegheny City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny,_Pennsylvania "Allegheny, Pennsylvania"), later to become part of [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Pennsylvania, in 1894. Her father, George Graham, was an "alienist", a practitioner of an early form of [psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatry "Psychiatry").[[3]](#cite_note-3) The Grahams were [Presbyterians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterians "Presbyterians"). Her father was a third-generation American of Irish descent. Graham's mother, Jane Beers, was a second-generation American of Irish, Scots-Irish, and English ancestry, and who claimed to be a tenth-generation descendant[[4]](#cite_note-4) of [Myles Standish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myles_Standish "Myles Standish").[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) While her parents provided a comfortable environment in her youth, it was not one that encouraged dancing.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199812-7)

The Graham family moved to [Santa Maria, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Maria,_California "Santa Maria, California"), when Martha was fourteen years old.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199820-8) In 1911, she attended the first dance performance of her life, watching [Ruth St. Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_St._Denis "Ruth St. Denis") perform at the [Mason Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_Opera_House "Mason Opera House") in Los Angeles.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFreedman199821-9) In the mid-1910s, Martha Graham began her studies at the newly created [Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denishawn_School_of_Dancing_and_Related_Arts "Denishawn School of Dancing and Related Arts"), founded by Ruth St. Denis and [Ted Shawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Shawn "Ted Shawn"),[[10]](#cite_note-BryantPratt94-10) at which she would stay until 1923. In 1922, Graham performed one of Shawn's Egyptian dances with [Lillian Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lillian_Powell "Lillian Powell") in a short silent film by [Hugo Riesenfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Riesenfeld "Hugo Riesenfeld") that attempted to synchronize a dance routine on film with a live orchestra and an onscreen conductor.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Martha_Graham&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Graham left the Denishawn establishment in 1923 in order to become a featured dancer in the [Greenwich Village Follies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village_Follies "Greenwich Village Follies") revue for two years.

In 1925, Graham was employed at the [Eastman School of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastman_School_of_Music "Eastman School of Music") where [Rouben Mamoulian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouben_Mamoulian "Rouben Mamoulian") was head of the School of Drama. Among other performances, together Mamoulian and Graham produced a short [two-color film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_motion_picture_film "Color motion picture film") called *The Flute of Krishna,* featuring Eastman students. Mamoulian left Eastman shortly thereafter and Graham chose to leave also, even though she was asked to stay on.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 1926, the [Martha Graham Center of Contemporary Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Center_of_Contemporary_Dance "Martha Graham Center of Contemporary Dance") was established, in a small studio on the [Upper East Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_East_Side "Upper East Side") of New York City. On April 18 of the same year[[10]](#cite_note-BryantPratt94-10) Graham debuted her first independent concert, consisting of 18 short solos and trios that she had choreographed. This performance took place at the [48th Street Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/48th_Street_Theatre "48th Street Theatre") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"). She would later say of the concert: "Everything I did was influenced by [Denishawn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denishawn "Denishawn")."[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMansfield_Soares199256-12) On November 28, 1926, Graham and others in her company gave a dance recital at the [Klaw Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klaw_Theatre "Klaw Theatre") in New York City. Around the same time she entered an extended collaboration with Japanese-American [pictorialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictorialism "Pictorialism") photographer [Soichi Sunami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soichi_Sunami "Soichi Sunami").[[13]](#cite_note-13) Graham was on the faculty of [Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood_Playhouse_School_of_the_Theatre "Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre") when it opened in 1928.[[14]](#cite_note-peck-14)

One of Graham's students was heiress [Bethsabée de Rothschild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethsabée_de_Rothschild "Bethsabée de Rothschild") with whom she became close friends. When Rothschild moved to Israel and established the [Batsheva Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batsheva_Dance_Company "Batsheva Dance Company") in 1965, Graham became the company's first director.[[15]](#cite_note-15)

[Graham's technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_technique "Graham technique") pioneered a principle known as "contraction and release" in modern dance, which was derived from a stylized conception of breathing.[[16]](#cite_note-CraineMackrell2010-16)

In conjunction with the [1936 Summer Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympic_Games "1936 Summer Olympic Games") in Berlin, the German government wanted to include dance in the Art Competitions that took place during the Olympics, an event that previously included architecture, sculpture, painting, music, and literature.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Although [Joseph Goebbels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Goebbels "Joseph Goebbels"), Reich Minister of Propaganda, was not appreciative of the modern dance art form and changed Germany's dance from more avant-garde to traditional, he and [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") still agreed to invite Graham to represent the United States. However, the United States was not represented in the Art Competitions as Graham refused the invitation by stating:

> I would find it impossible to dance in Germany at the present time. So many artists whom I respect and admire have been persecuted, have been deprived of the right to work for ridiculous and unsatisfactory reasons, that I should consider it impossible to identify myself, by accepting the invitation, with the regime that has made such things possible. In addition, some of my concert group would not be welcomed in Germany.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanley2004136-18)

Goebbels himself wrote her a letter assuring her that her Jewish dancers would "receive complete immunity". Graham nevertheless rejected the invitation.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHanley2004137-19)

Stimulated by the occurrences of the 1936 Olympic Games, and the propaganda that she heard through the radio from the [Axis powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers"), Graham created *[American Document](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Document "American Document")* in 1938. The dance expressed American ideals and democracy as Graham realized that it could empower men and inspire them to fight fascist and Nazi ideologies. American Document ended up as a patriotic statement focusing on rights and injustices of the time, representing the American people including its Native-American heritage and slavery. During the performance, excerpts from the [U.S. Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_Independence_(U.S.) "Declaration of Independence (U.S.)"), Lincoln's [Gettysburg Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettysburg_Address "Gettysburg Address"), and the [Emancipation Proclamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation "Emancipation Proclamation") were read. These were passages that highlighted the American ideals and represented what made the American people American. For Graham, a dance needed to "reveal certain national characteristics because without these characteristics the dance would have no validity, no roots, no direct relation to life".[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In 1938, the [Roosevelt family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roosevelt_family "Roosevelt family") invited Graham to dance at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House"), making her the first dancer to perform there.[[21]](#cite_note-21) In the same year, [Erick Hawkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erick_Hawkins "Erick Hawkins") became the first man to dance with her company. He officially joined her troupe the following year, dancing male lead in a number of Graham's works. They were married in July 1948 after the New York premiere of *Night Journey*.[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFranko2012139-22) He left her troupe in 1951 and they divorced in 1954.

On April 1, 1958, the [Martha Graham Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Dance_Company "Martha Graham Dance Company") premiered the ballet *[Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra_(dance) "Clytemnestra (dance)")*, which would become a success.[[23]](#cite_note-23) With a score by Egyptian-born composer [Halim El-Dabh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halim_El-Dabh "Halim El-Dabh"), this ballet was a large scale work and the only full-length work in Graham's career. Graham choreographed and danced the title role, spending almost the entire duration of the performance on the stage.[[24]](#cite_note-lamothe-24) The ballet tells the story of Queen [Clytemnestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clytemnestra "Clytemnestra"), who is married to King [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon").

Catalan cellist and conductor (1876–1973)

"Casals" redirects here. For other people with this surname, see [Casals (surname)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casals_(surname) "Casals (surname)"). For the medieval rural settlements, see [Casalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casalis "Casalis").

In this [Catalan name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_name "Catalan name"), the first or paternal [surname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surname "Surname") is  *Casals* and the second or maternal family name is  *Defilló*; both are generally joined by the conjunction "i".

**Pablo Casals** (29 December 1876 – 22 October 1973), also known by his birth name, **Pau Casals i Defilló** (Catalan: [[ˈpaw kəˈzalz i ðəfiˈʎo]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Catalan "Help:IPA/Catalan")), was a [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalonia "Catalonia") cellist, composer, and conductor, born in Spain. He made many recordings throughout his career of solo, chamber, and orchestral music, including some as conductor, but he is perhaps best remembered for the recordings he made of the [Cello Suites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello_Suites_(Bach) "Cello Suites (Bach)") by [Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach").

Casals had an international career and traveled and performed widely. With the fall of [Republican Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Spanish_Republic "Second Spanish Republic") to the [Nationalist forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist_faction_(Spanish_Civil_War) "Nationalist faction (Spanish Civil War)") of [Francisco Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Franco "Francisco Franco") in 1939, Casals went into self-exile, refusing to return to Spain until democracy was restored. He lived in [Prades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prades,_Pyrénées-Orientales "Prades, Pyrénées-Orientales"), France from 1939 to 1956, and then in [Ceiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceiba,_Puerto_Rico "Ceiba, Puerto Rico"), Puerto Rico from 1956 until his death in 1973.

[President John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_John_F._Kennedy "President John F. Kennedy") awarded Casals the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") in 1963, though the ceremony was presided over by President [Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson"). One of his last compositions was the *[Hymn to the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn_to_the_United_Nations "Hymn to the United Nations")*, which he conducted at the United Nations in 1971. At that event, he was awarded the U.N. Peace Medal in recognition of his stance for peace, justice and freedom. In accepting the award, he gave a short speech *[I Am a Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Am_a_Catalan "I Am a Catalan")* and performed the traditional Catalan song, *[El Cant dels Ocells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Cant_dels_Ocells "El Cant dels Ocells")* (Catalan: [[əl ˈkan dəlz uˈseʎs]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Catalan "Help:IPA/Catalan"), 'The Song of the Birds').

## Childhood and early years

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Pablo_Casals&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Childhood and early years")]

Casals was born in [El Vendrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Vendrell "El Vendrell"), [Catalonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalonia "Catalonia"), Spain. His father, Carles Casals i Ribes, was a parish [organist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organist "Organist") and [choirmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conducting "Conducting"). His mother, [Doña Pilar Defilló de Casals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilar_Defilló_Amiguet "Pilar Defilló Amiguet"), was born in [Mayagüez, Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayagüez,_Puerto_Rico "Mayagüez, Puerto Rico"), to parents who were [Catalan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalans "Catalans") immigrants in Puerto Rico.[[2]](#cite_note-casa-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Casals' father gave him instruction in piano, songwriting, violin, and organ. He was also a very strict disciplinarian. When Casals was young, his father would pull the piano out from the wall and have him and his brother, Artur, stand behind it and name the notes and the scales that his father was playing. At the age of four, Casals could play the violin, piano and flute; at the age of six he played the violin well enough to perform a solo in public. His first encounter with a cello-like instrument was from witnessing a local travelling [Catalan musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Catalonia "Music of Catalonia"), who played a cello-strung broom handle. Upon request, his father built him a crude cello, using a [gourd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gourd "Gourd") as a sound-box. When Casals was 11 years old, he first heard the real cello performed by a group of traveling musicians, and decided to dedicate himself to the instrument.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In 1888, Casals' mother took him to Barcelona, where he was enrolled in the Escola Municipal de Música.[[2]](#cite_note-casa-2) There he studied cello, theory, and piano. In 1890, when he was 13, he had a formative event. As he recalled,

> For two reasons I shall never forget that afternoon. First, my father bought me my first full-size cello – how proud I was to have that wonderful instrument! Then we stopped at an old music shop near the harbour [in Barcelona]. I began browsing through a bundle of musical scores. Suddenly I came upon a sheaf of pages, crumpled and discoloured with age. They were unaccompanied suites by [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach "Johann Sebastian Bach") – for the cello only! I looked at them with wonder: [Six Suites for Violoncello Solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cello_Suites_(Bach) "Cello Suites (Bach)"). What magic and mystery, I thought, were hidden in those words?... That scene has never grown dim.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

He spent the next 13 years practicing the Six Suites every day before he would perform them in public for the first time.[[5]](#cite_note-5) Casals would later make his own version of the six suites.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Written in the early 1700s, but only published in 1825, this preeminent work for the cello was largely neglected until it was rediscovered, performed, and recorded by Casals.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Casals made prodigious progress as a cellist. On 23 February 1891 he gave a solo recital in Barcelona at the age of fourteen. He graduated from the *Escola* with honours five years later.

## Youth and studies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Pablo_Casals&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Youth and studies")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Ramon_Casas_-_MNAC-_Pau_Casals-_027622-D_006612.jpg/250px-Ramon_Casas_-_MNAC-_Pau_Casals-_027622-D_006612.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramon_Casas_-_MNAC-_Pau_Casals-_027622-D_006612.jpg)

A young Pau Casals, by [Ramon Casas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Casas "Ramon Casas")

In 1893, Spanish composer [Isaac Albéniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Albéniz "Isaac Albéniz") heard him playing in a trio in a café and gave him a letter of introduction to the Count [Guillermo Morphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guillermo_Morphy "Guillermo Morphy"), the private secretary to [María Cristina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Christina_of_Austria "Maria Christina of Austria"), the Queen Regent of Spain. Casals was asked to play at informal concerts in the palace, and was granted a royal stipend to study composition at the [Madrid Royal Conservatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Royal_Conservatory "Madrid Royal Conservatory") in Madrid with [Víctor Mirecki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Víctor_Mirecki_Larramat "Víctor Mirecki Larramat"). He also played in the newly organised Quartet Society.

In 1895, he traveled to Paris, where, having lost his stipend[*[why?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")*], he earned a living by playing second cello in the theatre orchestra of the *[Folies Marigny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thétre_des_Folies-Marigny "Thétre des Folies-Marigny")*. In 1896, he returned to Spain and received an appointment to the faculty of the Escola Municipal de Música in Barcelona. He was also appointed principal cellist in the orchestra of Barcelona's opera house, the [Liceu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liceu "Liceu"). In 1897, he appeared as soloist with the [Madrid Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid_Symphony_Orchestra "Madrid Symphony Orchestra"), and was awarded the [Order of Carlos III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Charles_III "Order of Charles III") from the Queen. [*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

**Copland** is an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its floor is flooded with volcanic smooth plains material, which could be related to the activity that formed the nearby bright vent known as [Nathair Facula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathair_Facula "Nathair Facula").

## Naming

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Copland_(crater)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Naming")]

Amateur astronomer Ronald Dantowitz and his colleagues Scott Teare and Marek Kozubal used the Mt. Wilson 60-inch telescope in 1998 to observe a very bright feature on this portion of Mercury's surface, and they assumed that the bright feature was an impact crater. Mr. Dantowitz expressed his wish that the crater be named "Copland" (after American composer [Aaron Copland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Copland "Aaron Copland")) once better images of the area were obtained from spacecraft.

Surprisingly, *[MESSENGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESSENGER "MESSENGER")* images from Mercury flyby 3 revealed that the small bright feature, seen at the left edge of this image and now known as [Nathair Facula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathair_Facula "Nathair Facula"), is not an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") but more closely resembles a [volcanic vent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_vent "Volcanic vent"). No convention for naming volcanic vents on Mercury had yet been adopted, because none were identified prior to *MESSENGER*'s first Mercury flyby. A *MESSENGER* team member corresponded with Mr. Dantowitz and suggested that the name Copland be proposed instead for a large crater nearby. He agreed, and the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) approved the name Copland on March 3, 2010.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-IAU-2)

**Ellington** is a [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)") named after [Duke Ellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Ellington "Duke Ellington"), an American composer, pianist, and leader of a jazz orchestra. It was named by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in 2012.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Ellington is one of 110 [peak ring basins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_ring "Peak ring") on Mercury.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Within Ellington is the smaller crater [Berkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkel_(crater) "Berkel (crater)"). The somewhat smaller crater [Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derain_(crater) "Derain (crater)") is to the northwest. Both Derain and Ellington lie within a much older, 730-km-diameter, unnamed crater (referred to as b36).[[3]](#cite_note-3) The crater [Nasir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasir_(crater) "Nasir (crater)") is to the south of Ellington.

# Disney (crater)

Disney

| Coordinates | [68°09′S 260°12′W﻿ / ﻿68.15°S 260.2°W﻿ / -68.15; -260.2](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Disney_(crater)&params=68.15_S_260.2_W_globe:mercury_type:landmark) |

![}](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Disney-crater.png/330px-Disney-crater.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)
![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Disney_crater_labeled_by_NASA.png/250px-Disney_crater_labeled_by_NASA.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**Disney** is an [impact crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the H-15 (Bach) Quadrangle of [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)").[[1]](#cite_note-1) It was approved and adopted by the [IAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") on Dec 19, 2012.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Disney is 113 km (70 mi) in diameter. This crater was named after [Walt Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney "Walt Disney") (Walter Elias), the American entrepreneur, voice actor, film producer, and animator. Disney is one of many craters named after notable art figures; per the [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), Mercury's craters are all named after a famous artist, composer, or writer who was influential for more than 50 years and deceased for more than three years at the time the crater was named.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Disney was named months after [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") acknowledged it for its resemblance to [Mickey Mouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mickey_Mouse "Mickey Mouse").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

# Cunningham (crater)

Cunningham

|  |  |

![}](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Cunningham_crater_EN1010038848M.jpg/330px-Cunningham_crater_EN1010038848M.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

**Cunningham** is a young [crater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on the western floor of the [Caloris Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caloris_Basin "Caloris Basin"), on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It is surrounded by a bright [ray system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crater_ray "Crater ray").

The crater's name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in 2008, shortly after its discovery on the first flyby of [MESSENGER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MESSENGER "MESSENGER"). It is named for the American photographer [Imogen Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imogen_Cunningham "Imogen Cunningham").[[1]](#cite_note-1)

A confirmed *dark spot* is present in Cunningham crater.[[2]](#cite_note-2) This dark spot is associated with [hollows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollows_(Mercury) "Hollows (Mercury)").

Merce Cunningham

**Mercier "Merce" Philip Cunningham** (April 16, 1919– July 26, 2009) was an American dancer and choreographer who was at the forefront of American modern dance for more than 50 years. He frequently collaborated with artists of other disciplines, including musicians [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), [David Tudor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tudor "David Tudor"), [Brian Eno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Eno "Brian Eno"), and graphic artists [Robert Rauschenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Rauschenberg "Robert Rauschenberg"), [Bruce Nauman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Nauman "Bruce Nauman"), [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), [Roy Lichtenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Lichtenstein "Roy Lichtenstein"), [Frank Stella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Stella "Frank Stella"), and [Jasper Johns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jasper_Johns "Jasper Johns"); and fashion designer [Rei Kawakubo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rei_Kawakubo "Rei Kawakubo"). Works that he produced with these artists had a profound impact on avant-garde art beyond the world of dance.

As a choreographer, teacher, and leader of the Merce Cunningham Dance Company,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-2) Cunningham had a profound influence on [modern dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_dance "Modern dance"). Many dancers who trained with Cunningham formed their own companies. They include [Paul Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Taylor_(choreographer) "Paul Taylor (choreographer)"), [Remy Charlip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remy_Charlip "Remy Charlip"), [Viola Farber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_Farber "Viola Farber"), [Charles Moulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Moulton_(choreographer) "Charles Moulton (choreographer)"), [Karole Armitage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karole_Armitage "Karole Armitage"), [Deborah Hay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_Hay "Deborah Hay"), Robert Kovich, [Foofwa d'Imobilité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foofwa_d'Imobilit%C3%A9 "Foofwa d'Imobilité"), Kimberly Bartosik, [Flo Ankah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flo_Ankah "Flo Ankah"), [Jan Van Dyke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Van_Dyke "Jan Van Dyke"), [Jonah Bokaer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonah_Bokaer "Jonah Bokaer"), and [Alice Reyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Reyes "Alice Reyes").

In 2009, the Cunningham Dance Foundation announced the Legacy Plan, a plan for the continuation of Cunningham's work and the celebration and preservation of his artistic legacy.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-3)

Cunningham earned some of the highest honours bestowed in the arts, including the [National Medal of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Medal_of_Arts "National Medal of Arts") and the [MacArthur Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellows_Program "MacArthur Fellows Program"). He also received Japan's [Praemium Imperiale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praemium_Imperiale "Praemium Imperiale") and a British [Laurence Olivier Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Olivier_Awards "Laurence Olivier Awards"), and was named Officier of the [Légion d'honneur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9gion_d'honneur "Légion d'honneur") in France.

Cunningham's life and artistic vision have been the subject of numerous books, films, and exhibitions, and his works have been presented by groups including the [Paris Opéra Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Op%C3%A9ra_Ballet "Paris Opéra Ballet"), [New York City Ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Ballet "New York City Ballet"), [American Ballet Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Ballet_Theatre "American Ballet Theatre"), [White Oak Dance Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Oak_Dance_Project "White Oak Dance Project"), and London's [Rambert Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rambert_Dance_Company "Rambert Dance Company").

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Merce_Cunningham&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Merce Cunningham was born in [Centralia, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralia,_Washington "Centralia, Washington"), in 1919, the second of three sons. Both of his brothers followed their father, Clifford D. Cunningham,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-4) into the legal profession. Cunningham first experienced dance while living in Centralia. He took a [tap dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tap_dance "Tap dance") class from a local teacher, Mrs Maude Barrett, whose energy and spirit taught him to love dance. Her emphasis on precise musical timing and rhythm provided him with a clear understanding of musicality that he implemented in his later dance pieces.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-5) He attended the [Cornish College of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish_College_of_the_Arts "Cornish College of the Arts") in Seattle, headed by [Nellie Cornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nellie_Cornish "Nellie Cornish"), from 1937 to 1939 to study acting, but found drama's reliance on text and miming too limiting and concrete. Cunningham preferred the ambiguous nature of dance, which gave him an outlet for exploration of movement.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-6) During this time, [Martha Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham "Martha Graham") saw Cunningham dance and invited him to join her company.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-7) In 1939, Cunningham moved to New York City and danced as a soloist in the [Martha Graham Dance Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martha_Graham_Dance_Company "Martha Graham Dance Company") for six years. He presented his first solo concert in New York in April 1944 with composer [John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage "John Cage"), who became his lifelong romantic partner and frequent collaborator until Cage's death in 1992.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-8)

In the summer of 1953, as a teacher in residence at [Black Mountain College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Mountain_College "Black Mountain College"), Cunningham formed the Merce Cunningham Dance Company.

Throughout his career, Cunningham choreographed more than 200 dances and over 800 _Events_, or [site-specific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Site-specific_performance "Site-specific performance") choreographic works. In 1963 he joined with Cage to create the [Walker Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walker_Art_Center "Walker Art Center")'s first performance, instigating what would be a 25-year collaborative relationship with the Walker. In his performances, he often used the _[I Ching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Ching "I Ching")_ to determine the sequence of his dances and, often, dancers were not informed of the order until the night of the performance. In addition to his role as choreographer, Cunningham performed as a dancer in his company into the early 1990s.

In 1968 Cunningham published his book _Changes: Notes on Choreography_, edited by Francis Starr, containing various sketches of his choreography. A mural, located in Washington Hall on the campus of [Centralia College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centralia_College "Centralia College"), was created in honor of Cunningham.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-9)

Cunningham continued to live in New York City and lead his dance company as Artistic Director until his death. He presented his last work, a new work, _Nearly Ninety_, in April 2009, at the [Brooklyn Academy of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Academy_of_Music "Brooklyn Academy of Music"), New York, to mark his 90th birthday.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-10) Later that year he died in his home at the age of 90.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merce_Cunningham#cite_note-11)

**Morrison** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") in September 2022. Morrison is named for the American author [Toni Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toni_Morrison "Toni Morrison"), who lived from 1931 to 2019.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Morrison has a region of permanent shadow along its southern rim, which has a bright radar signature. This is interpreted to represent a deposit of water ice.[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3)

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Radar-bright_Deposits_near_Mercury%27s_North_Pole_messenger_orbit_image20120322.jpg/330px-Radar-bright_Deposits_near_Mercury%27s_North_Pole_messenger_orbit_image20120322.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

To the south of Morrison are the craters [Mansart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansart_(crater) "Mansart (crater)") and [Bjornson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bjornson_(crater) "Bjornson (crater)"). To the north are [Rizal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_(crater) "Rizal (crater)") and [Josetsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josetsu_(crater) "Josetsu (crater)"). To the east is [Despréz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despréz_(crater) "Despréz (crater)").

**Ailey** is a crater on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"). It has a diameter of 21 kilometers. Its name was adopted by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU) in on April 24, 2012. Ailey is named for the American dancer and choreographer [Alvin Ailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Ailey "Alvin Ailey"), who lived from 1931 to 1989.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Ailey is a fresh crater with a [ray system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_system "Ray system") that displays both low-reflectance material (LRM) and high-reflectance red material.[[2]](#cite_note-2)
